newsitem.title: USA: Russia's Mir space station trouble-prone since fire.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Mir space station trouble-prone since fire.

text.p: The collision of a cargo craft with Mir on Wednesday is the most serious in a string of difficulties to have hit the 11-year-old Russian space outpost.

Mir's trouble began with a major fire on Feb. 23, which filled the station with choking smoke. The fire, triggered by a chemical oxygen generator, burned for 14 minutes and blocked the route to a Soyuz escape ship docked at the station.
After that, the station's problems seemed to snowball, Jerry Linenger, NASA's Mir resident at the time, told Reuters in an interview earlier this month.
"After the fire, it seemed like every day something else was going wrong," he said.
Most of the problems were associated with the life support systems:
- The space station's primary oxygen generator failed, forcing the crew to rely on a chemical generator of the same type that triggered the February fire.

- Leaks in the cooling systems sent temperatures soaring to 96 degrees Fahrenheit (35.5 Celsius). The leaking antifreeze caused the crew to suffer breathing problems, allergic reactions and swollen eyes.
- The loss of cooling caused a device that cleans carbon dioxide from the cabin air to break down. The crew had to stop exercising and there was a buildup of condensation.
- A malfunction in the station's attitude control system caused it to list until a back-up system was activated.

- In an incident similar to Wednesday's collision, cosmonauts lost control of a cargo craft on March 4 as it approached Mir. The loss of television pictures used to remotely control the craft was blamed.
Most of Mir's problems were overcome when the same cargo craft that collided with the station on Wednesday arrived at Mir in April carrying repair gear.
The first part of Mir was launched in February 1986 and assembly of the station was completed in 1995.
